chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Khadir ibn Amr al-Nakha'i, who said:

One of the two Imams (peace be upon them) said regarding a man who has a debt due from another man who denies it: If he (the creditor) asks him to swear an oath, it is not for him to take anything from him after the swearing; and if he leaves it and does not ask him to swear, then he (the creditor) is upon his right.

key_terms.اسْتَحْلَفَهُ: he asked him to swear an oath

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a debtor denies a debt and swears an oath?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi details the mechanism of *istihlaf* (administering an oath) as a legal proof in Shia jurisprudence for settling debt disputes. It highlights the creditor's strategic choice: demanding an oath transfers the burden of proof to the debtor, and a successful oath discharges the debt, whereas withholding the oath preserves the creditor's original claim. This principle underscores the Shia emphasis on procedural justice and the evidentiary weight of oaths in civil transactions.
